Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Expectation2: Design and develop technical solutions to meet project requirements
Situation2: The build is stalled because no one can proceed until their core module is complete
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was deep in the final lines of code for the core module. The team’s messages were piling up—everyone was waiting on me to finish so the build could move forward. The pressure was intense; the deadline was looming, and I knew the project couldn’t afford another delay. Then, a video call request popped up from Sam. He sounded frazzled in his text: “Hey, can you hop on a quick call? I’m totally lost with this furniture, and I need to get it done tonight.” I could picture him surrounded by planks and screws, frustration mounting. As his friend, I wanted to be there for him, especially since he’d helped me out so many times before. But as an engineer, I was the bottleneck—my team was counting on me, and any distraction could set us back hours. My mind raced, torn between the urge to support my friend in his moment of need and the responsibility I felt toward my team and the project’s success. I stared at the two notifications, feeling the weight of both expectations pressing in from either side.
